title: Private Fears in Public Places
full_review:
The level of quality at which master French filmmaker Alain Resnais ("Last Year at Marienbad" and "Hiroshima, Mon Amour") continues to work, at a time when he might easily rest on proverbial laurels, continues to astonish. His last film, "Pas Sur La Bouche" ("Not on the Lips"), was a frothy and ultra-stylish concoction derived from a popular 1920s' Parisian operetta.

Now, "Private Fears in Public Places" ("Coeurs") (IFC First Take) is his superb reworking of British playwright Alan Ayckbourn's bittersweet stage comedy. The film is, in fact, his second adaptation of an Ayckbourn work.

This one concerns six characters, all trapped in their solitary lives, and all on a deep level searching for love. There's real estate agent Thierry (Andre Dussollier), who lives with his lovelorn sister Gaelle (Isabelle Carre). Unbeknownst to him, she goes out each night to rendezvous with men she's contacted through personal ads, though all end in disappointment.

Meanwhile, Thierry harbors feelings for his religiously minded secretary, Charlotte (Sabine Azema), whose proffered loans of "uplifting" videos (episodes of a spiritual program, "Songs That Changed My Life") are more than what they seem.

Charlotte moonlights as a companion to the ailing (and obscenely irascible) father of a widowed bartender, Lionel (Pierre Arditi), whose most steady customer is alcoholic ex-military man Dan (Lambert Wilson). The latter's relationship with frustrated girlfriend Nicole (Laura Morante) is plainly on the skids.

A humorous stage piece with a serious undertone here becomes a penetrating study of loneliness and alienation, and if memory serves little of the original dialogue has been changed.

Besides Resnais' assured direction, credit the sensitive performances of a terrific cast. (Arditi's first description about the estrangement from his father -- wonderfully subtle in its writing, too -- is breathtaking, to cite but one example.)

Mark Snow's evocative music and the rich production design add to the elegiac mood. One extraordinary conceit was setting the action in a snow-covered Paris. The ceaselessly falling flakes further emphasize the characters' solitude as all are enveloped in a quiet cocoon, as distancing as the walls, partitions and curtains which keep these characters -- so desperate for connection -- poignantly apart. (A surreal scene where the walls temporarily disappear as two characters converse at an indoor table, and the snow literally falls around them, speaks volumes about their desolation.)

Though Azema's character has proclivities wildly at odds with her pious demeanor, her imperfections pointedly represent the human flaws in all of us, while her faith is shown to be completely genuine. In fact, her observations on faith and the soul -- brief though they are -- register paradoxically as more spiritually profound than most of today's screen dialogue.

The film (screenplay by Jean-Michel Ribes) is a model of stage-to-screen adaptation, its measured, even formal, approach delivering an emotional punch that make it one of the most moving cinematic experiences of the year thus far.

Subtitles.

The film contains a brief suggestion of pornographic images, some rough and crude language, alcohol use, some domestic discord, and premarital situations and implied sexual activity.
